A signed-in first-time user enters the retained conversational setup and may globally Skip it. Keep the truthful rebranded opening, local/Firebase name, local/PostHog acquisition answer, local spoken-language choice, optional retained permission setup, global shortcuts, real skippable screen-aware PTT demo, meeting-only versus continuous-listening choice, local stage restoration/Back behavior, genuine-completion Home opener, and the individually retained presentation, reset and cleanup behavior.

Delete the unused role question; Full Disk Access and Automation stages; external agent/context connector stages; obsolete paged and AI-driven onboarding implementations; Agent VM, goal-generation and rejected cloud-write side effects; and every other child already rejected. Completion may enable only the separately retained local launch-at-login, capture and proactive behaviors. Skip remains a real consent-respecting exit and must not masquerade as completion.

This summary does not add a new onboarding screen, restore deleted Omi behavior, or override any child boundary.

### Code-grounded child-coverage audit

The production gate in `DesktopHomeView` mounts `SBOnboardingView` only when Firebase sign-in has succeeded and `hasCompletedOnboarding` is false. The active stage authority is `SBOnboardingModel.Step`, not the reconstructed requirement graph and not the legacy paged flow.

The active enum contains exactly 17 visible stages, and every case is represented by an existing child:

| Active Swift stage | Concrete code behavior | Existing child |
|---|---|---|
| `promise` | opening streamed promise, trust card, setup action | IR-126 |
| `name` | editable name, async profile update | IR-128/159 |
| `howHeard` | local category plus PostHog and current backend write | IR-124/129/159 |
| `language` | locale prefill, picker, local setting and current backend write | IR-071/130/159 |
| `role` | chips/free text and `onboardingRole` persistence | IR-131 |
| `mic` | native request, polling, pre-grant skip and optional bypass | IR-132 |
| `systemAudio` | Screen Recording prerequisite plus real tap verification | IR-133 |
| `screen` | TCC request/poll plus throwaway capture-consent prime | IR-134 |

| `accessibility` | native request, health checks, repair/polling and current broad copy | IR-136 |
| `automation` | AppleScript/System Events TCC trigger and polling | IR-137 |
| `shortcutOpen` | ⌘O/⌘Return choice, persistence and live rehearsal | IR-138/167 |

| `capture` | meeting-only versus continuous selection and completion | IR-127/143 through IR-148 |

The non-stage behavior is also mostly covered by source-backed children: global Skip (IR-127); post-completion opener (IR-144); Launch at Login and AppKit relaunch policy (IR-145 through IR-147); proactive monitoring (IR-148); resume, Back, streaming, no-progress and decorative transcript behavior (IR-149 through IR-153); superseded paged/AI-driven implementations and their persistence/test surfaces (IR-154 through IR-161); and Return, scrolling, layout, backdrop and disappearance cleanup (IR-162 through IR-169). The hidden completion calls to Agent VM and goal generation are already deleted by IR-001 and IR-027. The backend acquisition/language writes, Files scan and connector calls are explicitly removed by their listed children rather than silently surviving.

The cross-check found no unrepresented visible screen. It found three lifecycle behaviors outside `SBOnboardingModel.Step`, all now reviewed:

1. `OmiApp.shouldSkipOnboarding()` accepts `--skip-onboarding`, and `DesktopHomeView` directly sets the completion flag without calling either the retained global-Skip lifecycle or genuine completion. No repository script or test references this argument. This is IR-733.
2. `AppDelegate.applicationShouldTerminateAfterLastWindowClosed` returns true whenever onboarding is incomplete, so closing the onboarding window exits the complete menu-bar process; after onboarding, the same close leaves the app running. This is IR-734.
3. `SBOnboardingModel.begin()` and `DesktopHomeView` emit bounded state-authority diagnostics when the completion flag disagrees with the resume marker or onboarding journal, while still letting the completion flag win. This has a focused test but no requirement. This is IR-735.

Therefore IR-125 is closed: its visible stages and non-stage lifecycle behaviors all have explicit decisions.

## IR-126 - Active onboarding opening promise/trust screen

### Exact current screen from the code

After Firebase sign-in, when local `hasCompletedOnboarding` is false, `DesktopHomeView` renders `SBOnboardingView`. The first `.promise` step shows a streaming assistant message:

> Hey, I'm Omi, your second brain. I hear your conversations, remember everything, and handle the follow-ups. Three quick things:

It then shows this three-row trust card:

```text
OPEN      Every line of me is on GitHub.       -> links to BasedHardware/omi
PRIVATE   Your data is encrypted, and only yours.
YOURS     Pause me anytime. Delete anything, forever.
```

Visible actions:

- **Set up Omi →**: appends `Set me up` as the user's next chat bubble and advances to the name screen. It performs no permission, backend, or storage mutation itself.
- **Skip** in the top-right: exits the entire onboarding, records `onboardingCompleted`, presents the post-onboarding Home opener, clears the throwaway onboarding journal/drafts, and marks local onboarding complete. It does not grant permissions, enable screen analysis, or start continuous listening.

Presentation details:

- same image background as sign-in;
- assistant text streams word by word;
- there is no Back button on this first step;
- there are intentionally no progress dots or step count;
- the global Skip button remains visible throughout the later flow.

### Requirement materialized by this screen

> Before collecting any profile answer or requesting any Mac permission, explain the “Second Brain” promise and reassure the user about openness, privacy, control, and deletion; then let them enter or bypass setup.

### Code-grounded problems already visible

- The GitHub link points to Omi's repository, not this fork's eventual repository.
- “I hear your conversations, remember everything” was written for Omi's broader capture/sync product and must be checked against the final retained behavior.
- “Your data is encrypted, and only yours” is too broad to accept blindly because retained account, billing, transient AI/STT, and telemetry still send bounded data to services we operate.
- “Delete anything, forever” must match the retained local deletion and durable account-deletion behaviors.
- Calling Skip `onboardingCompleted` makes analytics unable to distinguish completing setup from bypassing it; whether Skip survives is a separate cross-screen behavior even though its button first appears here.

### Choices for this concrete screen

1. **Keep the opening screen structure.** Retain a short promise/trust screen before the name screen, but rebrand it and rewrite every claim after the architecture decisions are complete so the copy is literally true.
2. **Delete this screen.** After sign-in, the active flow begins immediately at the name screen. Trust/privacy explanations must then live beside the specific permission or data action they describe.

### Recommendation

`keep the opening screen structure, but do not keep its current Omi branding, link, or unverified absolute claims`

This screen gives context before later sensitive permission requests and costs little behaviorally. The exact trust copy is not approved by keeping the screen; it must be rewritten against the final local/cloud boundary. Audit the global Skip action separately because it affects every onboarding step.

### Question

Should we keep this first promise/trust screen before the name screen, with later rebranding and fact-checked copy, or delete the screen entirely?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the opening promise/trust screen, then rebrand and fact-check its claims against the final architecture`

Retain the opening conversational message, three-row trust card, primary setup action, simple presentation, and normal progression into the next screen. Replace Omi/product/repository identities, including the BasedHardware GitHub link. Rewrite the absolute privacy, memory, pause, and deletion claims only after the retained local/cloud architecture is final so the shipped copy is literally accurate.

This decision does not retain the global Skip behavior or any later onboarding screen by implication. Those remain separate concrete reviews under IR-125.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-127 - Global Skip action across active onboarding

### Exact current behavior from the code

The top-right **Skip** button is rendered outside the individual step widgets, so it appears on every active onboarding screen: the opening promise, profile questions, permission setup, shortcuts, demos, context setup, and the final capture choice.

Its tooltip says:

> Skip onboarding and go to your second brain

Clicking it immediately calls `SBOnboardingModel.skip()` and:

1. cancels onboarding-owned streaming, scans, polling, shortcut monitoring, and the voice demo;
2. reports the same PostHog **Onboarding Completed** event used by normal completion;
3. stops the temporary main-chat agent;
4. marks onboarding as locally completed and deletes the saved resume position;
5. presents the personalized post-onboarding Home opener;
6. clears the temporary onboarding journal and both onboarding chat drafts; and
7. leaves the onboarding UI and enters the product.

Unlike normal completion, Skip deliberately does **not**:

- apply the launch-at-login choice;
- generate the initial Goals insight;
- enable proactive screen analysis;
- start continuous transcription;
- reconcile capture; or
- start the Agent VM pipeline, which is already rejected under IR-001.

Therefore a user who presses Skip reaches Home with the permissions and capture features they bypassed still off. They can enable retained capabilities later through their normal controls.

### Requirement materialized by this behavior

> A first-time user must be able to abandon the entire setup from any point and enter Home without granting permissions or enabling capture.

### What is good and what is wrong

- The bypass respects consent: a long onboarding containing sensitive Mac permissions must not trap the user.
- It does not secretly enable microphone, screen analysis, or continuous recording after the user skips them.
- Because the button is global, it also lets a user abandon setup after supplying only some answers or permissions.
- The analytics are factually wrong: a bypassed flow is reported as **Onboarding Completed**, so PostHog cannot distinguish successful setup from abandonment.
- The personalized Home opener after a skip is another concrete behavior and is not automatically retained by keeping Skip.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Keep global Skip on every step.** Preserve the immediate consent-respecting exit, but report a separate **Onboarding Skipped** event instead of pretending the flow was completed.
2. **Remove global Skip.** Users may bypass individual optional choices, but they must travel through the remaining screens and explicitly finish the flow before entering Home.

### Recommendation

`keep global Skip on every step, preserve the current no-permission/no-capture exit, and report it as skipped rather than completed`

The flow currently contains many screens and several sensitive permission requests. A user should always be able to leave. The correction is small and truthful: keep the local completion flag that prevents onboarding from reopening automatically, but send a distinct analytics event so we know the setup was bypassed.

Treat the post-skip Home opener as a separate child requirement when we reach the completion/landing branch.

### Question

Should we keep the top-right Skip button on every onboarding screen, allowing the user to enter Home with skipped permissions and capture still off, while changing its PostHog event from **Onboarding Completed** to **Onboarding Skipped**?

### Decision

`resolved - keep global Skip and distinguish bypass from completion in analytics`

Retain the top-right Skip action on every active onboarding step. It must continue to enter Home without force-enabling any permission, capture, continuous transcription, or screen-analysis behavior that the user bypassed. Keep the local completed flag so the discarded setup does not automatically reopen.

Replace the misleading PostHog **Onboarding Completed** emission in `skip()` with a distinct **Onboarding Skipped** event. Normal completion keeps **Onboarding Completed**. Whether Skip should present the current personalized Home opener remains a separate completion/landing decision.

#### Later lifecycle correction discovered during IR-143

The earlier method-level reading was incomplete. `skip()` does not directly call `startTranscription()` or `startMonitoring()`, but `AssistantSettings` registers both `transcriptionEnabled` and `screenAnalysisEnabled` with default value `true`. After `hasCompletedOnboarding` reveals Home, `DesktopHomeView.restorePersistedCaptureServices()` reads those intents and can start transcription and proactive screen monitoring if the relevant permission/provider checks pass.

Therefore the current surrounding lifecycle can violate the approved Skip contract even though `skip()` itself avoids the start calls. Implementing this decision requires the Skip path to leave both capture intents explicitly off—or otherwise fence Home restoration—before the product UI appears. A user who bypasses setup must not receive a new Microphone prompt or have meeting-gated audio/screen monitoring start merely because the registered defaults are true.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-128 - Onboarding name question and profile persistence

### Exact current screen from the code

After the retained opening trust screen, onboarding asks:

> What should I call you?

The widget is one plain text field with placeholder **your name** and one arrow button. Return and the arrow perform the same action. Blank or whitespace-only input cannot advance, although the global Skip action can still leave onboarding.

Before the screen appears, the model tries to prefill the field from `AuthService.givenName`. If that local value is empty, it asynchronously loads a name from the backend Firestore user profile, then falls back to the Firebase Auth display name. An asynchronously arriving name fills only an empty field and never overwrites text the user has started typing.

After submission, onboarding immediately advances to **How did you hear about Omi?** while a serialized background write calls `AuthService.updateGivenName()`.

### Exact current write path

The submitted text is split into a first name and the remaining family name, then copied to three places:

```text
onboarding name answer
  -> local UserDefaults: auth_givenName + auth_familyName
  -> Firebase Auth: current user's displayName
  -> Python backend PATCH /v1/users/profile
       -> intended Firestore users/{uid}.name copy
```

Both remote writes are best-effort: the screen has already advanced, and a failure is logged without showing an error to the user.

There is concrete repository drift: the Mac declares and calls `PATCH /v1/users/profile`, but the current Python router exposes only `GET /v1/users/profile`; no matching PATCH handler exists in this checkout. Therefore the extra backend-name update appears to fail and adds a dependency without currently providing the claimed persistence.

### Where the name is actually used

This answer is not dead onboarding data. Current Mac code reads the local name for:

- the Home greeting, such as **Hey Sam. I'm ready.**;
- the personalized post-onboarding opener;
- the local **about user** context supplied to Chat;
- onboarding's later personalized copy; and
- Memory/atlas presentation.

The requirement materialized by the screen is therefore:

> Let the user confirm or change the name the assistant uses, then retain it for personalized local product behavior and future signed-in sessions.

### Choices for this concrete screen and side effect

1. **Keep the name screen, with one account-backed copy.** Prefill from local/Firebase Auth, let the user confirm or change it, keep the local name for fast product reads, and update our Firebase Auth display name so it can survive reinstall/sign-in. Delete the redundant backend `/v1/users/profile` name read/write path and Firestore `name` copy.
2. **Delete the name screen.** Use the Firebase/OAuth display name automatically when available and use a neutral greeting when it is missing. The user would need some later account setting if they want to change what the assistant calls them.
3. **Keep all three current stores.** Preserve local, Firebase Auth, and backend Firestore name copies, which also means repairing and maintaining the missing backend PATCH route plus reconciliation among them.

### Recommendation

`keep the name screen and its real personalization, but use local storage plus our retained Firebase Auth profile; delete the redundant backend profile-name copy`

OAuth names are not always present or are not what someone wants an assistant to call them, so this one-field confirmation has real value. Local storage keeps product behavior immediate. Firebase Auth is already retained for accounts and gives the name one durable account-level home. A second custom Firestore copy provides no distinct retained behavior, currently has no working PATCH route, and creates synchronization work.

This decision is only about the human-facing account/display name. It does not retain the separate AI user profile, memories, role answer, or other onboarding answers.

### Question

Should we keep this **What should I call you?** screen, save the chosen name locally and in our Firebase Auth account profile, and delete the duplicate Python-backend/Firestore name copy?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the name screen with local and Firebase Auth ownership; delete the backend profile-name copy`

Retain **What should I call you?**, its editable prefill, blank-input guard, and downstream local personalization. Save the chosen first/family name locally for immediate Mac behavior and update the retained Firebase Auth `displayName` as the durable account-level copy.

Delete the redundant Python-backend `/v1/users/profile` name read/write path and Firestore `users/{uid}.name` authority. On sign-in or reinstall, seed the local name from Firebase Auth rather than reconciling a third profile store. This does not retain other onboarding-profile or AI-profile fields.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-132 - Onboarding Microphone permission screen

### Exact current screen from the code

After the profile questions, onboarding says:

> Let's give me senses. First, your microphone, so I hear your side of a conversation.

It shows a card labeled:

```text
Microphone
hears your side of conversations
```

If permission is not granted, the user sees **Allow Microphone** and **Skip for now**. If it is already granted, onboarding skips this stage while advancing from the previous screen; if the user navigates back to it, the card shows **Microphone on** and **Continue**.

### Exact Allow behavior

Clicking **Allow Microphone**:

1. rechecks the current macOS permission so it does not prompt twice;
2. activates the app and calls the native `AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .audio)` prompt;
3. changes the card to **Waiting for macOS…**;
4. polls the local TCC result every half-second for up to about 20 seconds;
5. on grant, briefly displays success and automatically advances to System Audio; and
6. on timeout or denial, restores the Allow button instead of trapping the screen.

Clicking **Skip for now** records only the conversational answer `Skip` and advances. It does not grant anything or start capture.

Granting the permission during onboarding also does **not** start recording. `AppState.requestMicrophonePermission()` starts transcription only when onboarding has already completed. The later capture-choice/completion behavior decides whether listening begins.

All of this is local macOS permission handling. It does not write the permission state to Firestore or the Python backend.

### Requirement materialized by this screen

> Before the user reaches the product, explain and optionally obtain the native Microphone grant required for their side of continuous meeting transcription and PTT voice input.

### Why the permission still has a real consumer

Microphone access is required by two separately retained capabilities:

- continuous Mac meeting/conversation transcription; and
- push-to-talk/realtime spoken Chat.

IR-019/054 retain those parent capabilities, and IR-107 already retains the local native Microphone check/request tool. The open question here is narrower: whether onboarding should request the grant during setup or defer it until the first time the user turns on listening/PTT.

### Choices for this concrete screen

1. **Keep the current optional onboarding screen.** Explain the reason, allow the native grant, skip it when already granted, allow **Skip for now**, and do not start recording until the later explicit capture choice.
2. **Delete this onboarding screen.** Request Microphone permission only when the user first enables continuous transcription or starts PTT. The retained Settings/permission-repair paths still exist.

### Recommendation

`keep the current optional Microphone permission screen`

This is setup for two central retained behaviors, not a dead Omi/cloud dependency. The current implementation has good consent boundaries: the request is explained, skippable, purely local, never treats denial as completion, and granting permission alone does not begin recording. It also avoids interrupting the first PTT or meeting with a surprise system prompt.

Rebrand the product copy later, but keep the specific explanation about capturing the user's side of a conversation.

### Question

Should we keep this optional Microphone permission screen in onboarding, including **Skip for now** and the guarantee that granting it does not start recording yet?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the optional Microphone permission screen without starting capture`

Retain the explanation, native local permission request, live grant recheck, already-granted skip, bounded polling, automatic advance after success, and **Skip for now** path. Granting Microphone access during onboarding must continue to update permission state only; it must not start transcription or recording before the later explicit capture choice.

The retained screen has no backend authority or synchronization. Rebrand its product copy later while preserving the concrete explanation that Microphone access captures the user's side of a conversation.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-133 - Onboarding System Audio permission screen

### Exact current screen from the code

After Microphone, onboarding says:

> Now system audio, so I hear the other side too: Zoom, Meet, calls.

The card reads:

```text
System audio
the other side — Zoom, Meet, calls
```

Like Microphone, it offers **Allow System audio** and **Skip for now** when access is not confirmed. A previously confirmed grant skips the stage. The user can continue onboarding without it, but retained meeting transcription will then hear only the microphone side until system audio is enabled later.

### Why its permission flow is unusual

On macOS 14.4 and later, Core Audio process taps capture other applications' audio. macOS does not expose a trustworthy idle preflight for this access. The code therefore treats a short real tap attempt as the authoritative check.

Clicking **Allow System audio** currently:

1. rechecks local Screen Recording/System Audio state;
2. if Screen Recording consent is absent, opens its native request/System Settings pane because the capture permissions share that macOS privacy boundary;
3. polls only while the user remains on this stage;
4. after the macOS grant appears, starts and immediately stops a real Core Audio process tap;
5. marks System Audio on only when that tap succeeds; and
6. briefly shows success and automatically advances.

A failed tap resets the button so the user can retry. A late permission result cannot yank onboarding forward after the user has left the stage. On macOS versions older than 14.4, the feature is marked unsupported and the normal forward flow skips this request.

This verification does not start continuous capture. It tests access, stops the tap, and stores only process-local permission state. The later capture selection and local `systemAudioCaptureMode` decide when real recording runs.

### Requirement materialized by this screen

> During setup, optionally verify that the app can capture other applications' audio so meeting transcription records both the user and remote participants instead of producing a microphone-only transcript.

### Surviving product dependency

The Omi BLE path is deleted, but this is unrelated to BLE. It belongs to retained Mac capture:

```text
Mac microphone                         -> user's side
Core Audio process tap + local mixer  -> Zoom/Meet/call side
combined audio                         -> retained transcription lifecycle
```

Without System Audio, continuous meeting transcription still runs but normally misses remote speakers unless their sound leaks back through the physical microphone.

### Choices for this concrete screen

1. **Keep the optional onboarding verification.** Explain why it is needed, test the real tap, skip the stage when already granted/unsupported, keep **Skip for now**, and leave actual recording off until the later capture choice.
2. **Delete this onboarding screen.** Let the first meeting or later Settings action encounter and repair missing System Audio access. Microphone-only transcription remains the fallback until then.

### Recommendation

`keep the optional System Audio permission screen and its real-tap verification`

Hearing only the user's side would make the retained meeting-transcription product appear broken. This permission is harder to diagnose than Microphone because there is no reliable preflight, and the current short tap verifies the real path before the first meeting. The screen remains skippable, local, version-aware, and does not start ongoing recording.

The adjacent Screen Recording screen has a different retained purpose—Rewind/Focus and visual context—and will be challenged separately even though macOS permission plumbing overlaps.

### Question

Should we keep this optional System Audio screen so onboarding can verify the app will hear remote meeting participants, while retaining **Skip for now** and keeping ongoing recording off until the later capture choice?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the optional System Audio screen and real-tap verification`

Retain the concrete explanation about hearing remote meeting participants, the local Screen Recording prerequisite check, the short authoritative Core Audio tap test on supported macOS versions, retry/timeout safeguards, already-granted/unsupported bypass, automatic advance after success, and **Skip for now**.

The verification tap must stop immediately and must not begin continuous recording. The later explicit capture selection remains the authority for ongoing listening and the local System Audio mode.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

### Exact current screen from the code

### Exact Allow behavior

Clicking **Allow Screen Recording**:

1. rechecks `CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess()` locally;
2. activates and registers the current app build with Launch Services so macOS grants the correct bundle rather than a stale development copy;
3. calls the native Screen Recording request and ScreenCaptureKit enumeration request;
4. opens the correct Privacy & Security pane with the local drag-to-grant helper;
5. polls the TCC grant every half-second for about 20 seconds;
6. when granted, performs one best-effort 2×2 throwaway ScreenCaptureKit capture so macOS surfaces its additional direct-capture/private-picker consent during setup; and
7. automatically advances after briefly showing success.

The 2×2 prime is discarded in memory. It is not saved locally or uploaded. Granting permission does not itself turn on Rewind monitoring, proactive analysis, or PTT screenshot delivery. Those retained features have their own enablement and invocation rules.

If the user chooses **Skip for now**, the screen advances without the grant. Rewind, visual proactive assistance, and screen-aware Chat/PTT then degrade or show their existing permission-repair UI when used.

### Requirement materialized by this screen

> During setup, optionally obtain the macOS screen-capture grant needed by the product's retained visual features so their first use is not interrupted by System Settings and additional capture consent.

### Retained consumers

This permission is not kept merely because System Audio happens to share part of its TCC plumbing. It has separately retained consumers:

- Rewind screen capture and local OCR/history;
- precise Rewind/Focus behavior together with the retained Accessibility path;
- proactive screen analysis and the proactive overlay;
- typed Chat screen tools; and
- PTT current-screen evidence when the user asks a visual question.

The grant is local macOS state. Individual screenshots may later follow the already-reviewed local/transient model boundaries of those features, but onboarding does not synchronize the permission or captured prime image to the backend.

### Choices for this concrete screen

1. **Keep the optional onboarding screen.** Explain the visual purpose, avoid duplicate prompting after System Audio, retain **Skip for now**, and prime the real ScreenCaptureKit consent without enabling ongoing monitoring.
2. **Delete this onboarding screen.** Request Screen Recording only when the user first enables Rewind/proactive capture or asks a screen-dependent Chat/PTT question. Existing repair paths remain.

### Recommendation

`keep the optional Screen Recording permission screen`

Multiple retained first-release behaviors require this sensitive grant, and macOS may involve both a Settings toggle and a later direct-capture prompt. Handling those steps in an explained, skippable setup screen avoids making Rewind or the first visual question appear broken. The current code also avoids a second screen when System Audio already obtained the grant.

Rebrand the copy later and keep it precise about retained screen-reading behavior; do not restore deleted clicking, typing, connector automation, or general computer control.

### Question

Should we keep this optional Screen Recording permission screen for Rewind/Focus, proactive assistance, and screen-aware Chat/PTT, including **Skip for now** and no automatic ongoing monitoring merely from granting it?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the optional Screen Recording permission screen without enabling monitoring`

Retain the local native request, correct-bundle registration, System Settings guidance, live TCC polling, already-granted bypass, **Skip for now**, and best-effort throwaway ScreenCaptureKit consent prime. The prime image remains discarded and must never be saved or uploaded.

Granting Screen Recording access by itself must not enable Rewind capture, proactive monitoring, or screenshot delivery. Those retained behaviors remain controlled by their own local settings, invocations, and the later completion audit. Rebrand and narrow the copy to the final retained visual capabilities without restoring deleted actuation.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-138 - Onboarding global open-assistant shortcut screen

### Exact current screen from the code

After the surviving permission stages, onboarding asks:

> How do you want to open me? Just press one of these to set it.

It offers only two global shortcuts:

```text
⌘ O    tap to open
⌘ ↩    tap to open
```

The user may click a row or simply press either offered combination. The moment a combination is recognized, onboarding saves it to local `ShortcutSettings.askOmiShortcut` and enables the global Ask-Omi shortcut. It then asks the user to tap it and displays **Perfect, that works.** before showing Continue. **Skip for now** is always available.

The setting remains editable, recordable as a custom combination, or disableable later in Settings.

### What the screen is trying to guarantee

> A first-time user should choose, learn, and physically rehearse the system-wide keyboard shortcut that summons the assistant from another Mac application.

That is a real desktop behavior: `GlobalShortcutManager` registers the saved combination through Carbon and opens the assistant window when it fires.

### Concrete problems in the current implementation

1. **The shortcut is not actually optional by default.** `ShortcutSettings` defaults to enabled with global ⌘O before this screen is answered. Pressing **Skip for now** without choosing anything leaves that global default active.
2. **⌘O is the standard macOS Open command.** Registering it globally can take a familiar application shortcut away from whichever app the user is working in.
3. **The onboarding test is not authoritative.** While this stage is visible, the real Carbon hotkey is suspended and local/global event monitors merely observe the keystroke. They can show **Perfect, that works** even if Carbon later rejects the shortcut because another app already owns it.
4. **Registration failure is not shown to the user.** The production registration path logs/reports the failure, but the onboarding screen already declared success.
5. **Choosing a row saves and enables it immediately.** If the user then presses **Skip for now** instead of testing, the selected global shortcut remains active; Skip means skip the rehearsal, not undo the choice.

### Choices for this concrete requirement

1. **Keep the onboarding shortcut setup, but make it explicit and truthful.** Start unconfigured/disabled for a new user, offer a conflict-resistant preset or the existing custom recorder, attempt the real Carbon registration before claiming success, and make **Skip for now** leave the open-assistant shortcut disabled. Keep later Settings control.
2. **Delete this onboarding screen but keep the feature in Settings.** Do not enable a global open shortcut by default; users who want one configure it later. The menu bar/notch/main window remains the discovery path.
3. **Keep the screen and defaults unchanged.** Continue globally enabling ⌘O by default and treating observed onboarding keystrokes as proof that registration works.

### Recommendation

`keep a simple onboarding setup for the global open-assistant shortcut, but require explicit opt-in and validate the real registered hotkey`

A system-wide summon is valuable and easy to miss if buried in Settings, so the screen earns its place. But silently claiming the standard ⌘O shortcut and showing a false-positive success message violates the purpose of setup. Reuse the existing Shortcut Settings custom-recording and Carbon registration machinery rather than inventing a second shortcut system.

This decision concerns only the tap-to-open shortcut. The following hold-to-talk shortcut is a separate screen and already has its own retained PTT requirements.

### Question

Should we keep this onboarding screen for choosing the global open-assistant shortcut, but make it explicit opt-in, use a conflict-resistant/custom choice, verify the real Carbon registration before saying it works, and leave the feature disabled when the user presses **Skip for now**?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the open-assistant shortcut screen unchanged`

Retain the current ⌘O and ⌘Return choices, default-enabled ⌘O behavior, immediate local persistence/enabling on selection, event-monitor rehearsal, **Perfect, that works** success condition, and existing **Skip for now** semantics. Do not change this stage to explicit opt-in, disable the default on skip, replace the presets, add custom recording here, or gate its success label on the later Carbon registration outcome.

The identified standard-⌘O conflict and possible difference between onboarding event observation and later Carbon registration remain documented context, not authorized changes. Later Settings customization and disable controls remain intact.

## IR-140 - Live screen-aware PTT onboarding demo

### Exact current screen from the code

Entering this stage:

6. displays the real floating notch/bar;
7. waits for the configured hold-to-talk shortcut; and
8. marks the demo complete only after a real AI response becomes visible or starts speaking.

The spoken turn follows the retained production PTT path. The microphone audio goes to the selected realtime/model path, and the suggested visual question can cause current-screen evidence to be sent to that model under the already-reviewed screen-sharing rules. This is therefore a real provider interaction with real latency/cost, not a local animation.

All onboarding chat/voice turns are routed to a temporary `.onboarding()` local journal plus onboarding-only floating/main drafts. They are kept out of the user's normal Chat history and cleared when onboarding completes or is globally skipped.

Leaving the demo cancels unfinished warmup/setup, removes the response observer, clears demo UI, restores the user's saved PTT transcription mode, cleans up demo PTT monitors, and hides the borrowed floating bar. A late warmup cannot attach PTT to a later onboarding stage.

2. **Delete the demo stage.** Shortcut selection remains, but the user's first real PTT turn happens naturally after onboarding. Remove the demo-only bridge warmup, draft switching, transcription-mode override, response observation, UI state, teardown, and tests.
3. **Replace it with a fake/local tutorial.** Animate the shortcut and floating bar without sending audio or screen evidence. This reduces failure/cost but no longer proves the production path and requires new demo behavior.

### Recommendation

`keep the current skippable live screen-aware PTT demo`

PTT plus screen context is a central retained interaction and not obvious from static copy. This stage both teaches the gesture and validates the full chain before the user depends on it elsewhere. The implementation already limits the cost/risk: it can be skipped, uses temporary local history, does not persist its forced live mode, retries failed warmup, and tears down its real runtime ownership when the stage ends.

IR-061 now keeps both realtime providers, so the demo may exercise whichever configured OpenAI Realtime or Gemini Live path is primary at that moment. IR-113 separately keeps the current managed-Claude path for normal typed Chat.

`resolved - keep the current skippable live screen-aware PTT demo`

Retain the production-path bridge warmup, temporary live-transcription override, real floating bar, configured PTT gesture, screen-aware provider turn, retry/unavailable state, Continue-after-real-answer behavior, always-available pre-answer Skip, isolated onboarding journal/drafts, and lifecycle-fenced teardown. ## IR-143 - Final onboarding listening-mode choice

### Exact current screen from the code

After connector setup, onboarding says:

> You're all set, Sam. One last thing: should I listen all the time, or only during your meetings?

It offers two buttons:

```text
● Only during meetings · from my calendar     [default/primary]
Start listening — continuously
```

There is no third **Do not listen** choice on this screen, although the global top-right Skip remains available and listening can later be turned off from Home, the menu bar, or Settings.

### Exact choice behavior

**Only during meetings** stores local `systemAudioCaptureMode = onlyDuringMeetings`. Once the transcription session is armed, `MeetingDetector` polls every four seconds for supported conferencing apps using their microphone or for browser call-window titles. Outside a detected meeting, both microphone and System Audio capture remain off. During a detected meeting, both start; after an eight-second end grace period they stop and the conversation is finalized.

The button's **from my calendar** claim is false. The retained detector does not consult calendar events to decide when capture begins.

**Start listening — continuously** stores local `systemAudioCaptureMode = always` and directly starts transcription during completion. In this mode the microphone runs continuously and System Audio follows the always-on mode until the user turns listening off or changes mode.

Both choices are local settings. They do not synchronize the capture mode to Firestore. The chosen transcription engine can still be local Parakeet or the retained `/v4/listen` fallback under IR-019.

### Important boundary with completion

Pressing either button immediately calls the broader completion routine, which also performs analytics, clears onboarding history, enters Home, generates initial Goals output, applies launch-at-login state, enables proactive screen analysis, and currently starts the rejected Agent VM. Those side effects are **not** approved merely by keeping this listening choice; each will be audited separately after this screen decision.

### Requirement materialized by this screen

> Before onboarding ends, require the user to choose whether retained audio transcription should wait for detected meetings or capture continuously.

### Choices for this concrete screen

1. **Keep both listening modes, with meeting-only as the recommended default.** Retain the explicit choice and local mode setting, but rewrite **from my calendar** to truthfully say the app detects supported calls. Keep the global Skip/no-capture path.
2. **Keep only meeting-only listening.** Remove continuous capture from onboarding while retaining its later Settings control.
3. **Delete the screen.** Default new users to meeting-only and let them change/enable listening later from Home or Settings.

### Recommendation

`keep the explicit two-mode choice, keep meeting-only as the primary recommendation, and correct the calendar claim`

IR-018 already retained automatic meeting-gated listening and its onboarding UI. Continuous listening is a materially more sensitive behavior, so it should not be silently selected by a default. Showing both choices makes that distinction explicit while still steering users to the narrower meeting-only mode. The only required copy correction is to describe real local call detection rather than a calendar dependency that the code does not use.

The global Skip behavior must honor IR-127 by leaving transcription and screen-analysis intent off; it is not a hidden third choice that restores default-enabled capture after Home appears.

### Question

Should we keep this final two-button choice with **Only during detected meetings** as the primary option and **Start listening continuously** as the explicit alternative, while removing the false **from my calendar** claim?

### Decision

`resolved - keep both listening modes, meeting-only primary, with truthful call-detection copy`

Retain the final explicit choice between local `.onlyDuringMeetings` and `.always` modes. Keep meeting-only as the primary/default action and continuous listening as the deliberate alternative. Replace **from my calendar** with copy that truthfully explains supported-call detection through conferencing-app/microphone/browser-title signals.

Meeting-only must arm the retained transcription session while keeping microphone and System Audio capture off outside a detected call. Continuous begins capture immediately. Global Skip remains a separate no-capture outcome under IR-127. This decision does not approve unrelated completion side effects.

## IR-145 - Implicit Launch at Login mutation on onboarding completion

### Exact current behavior from the code

`SBOnboardingModel` contains:

```swift
var launchAtLogin: Bool = LaunchAtLoginManager.shared.isEnabled
```

Normal completion later calls `applyLaunchAtLoginSelection()`, which sends that stored Boolean back to `SMAppService.mainApp.register()` or `.unregister()` and emits a PostHog **Launch at Login Changed** event on success.

The current active Second Brain onboarding has no Launch at Login screen, toggle, button, or other binding. Nothing in the flow changes `model.launchAtLogin`, so the field and completion helper have no active UI owner.

### Why the stored value is not a reliable “user selection”

`LaunchAtLoginManager.isEnabled` begins as `false` and asynchronously reads the actual `SMAppService.mainApp.status`. The onboarding model copies the current published Boolean once during initialization; it does not observe later status updates.

Therefore:

```text
model initializes before async system-status read completes
  -> model.launchAtLogin captures false

actual Mac login item may already be enabled
  -> manager later publishes true
  -> model's copied value remains false

user completes onboarding
  -> completion calls setEnabled(false)
  -> existing login item can be unregistered
```

Even when the snapshot happens to be accurate, rewriting the same system preference and reporting it as a change provides no onboarding behavior because the user never made a choice.

The focused tests prove that the helper forwards `true` or `false`; they do not prove that active onboarding collected a current user selection. Their comments still describe a choice that this flow does not render.

### Adjacent Launch at Login behaviors are separate branches

Deleting or retaining this onboarding-completion mutation does not delete the Launch at Login feature:

- Settings has a real toggle bound to the observed `LaunchAtLoginManager` system status and reports only a user-initiated change.
- `OmiApp.migrateLaunchAtLoginDefault()` is a separate one-time path that can enable the login item for an already-onboarded local profile. Its own requirement and stale asynchronous status read still need a separate challenge.
- `NSApp.enableRelaunchOnLogin()` / `disableRelaunchOnLogin()` is another macOS lifecycle policy around onboarding and non-production bundles. It is not the same `SMAppService` login-item setting and is not decided by IR-145.

### Requirement materialized by the retained listening lifecycle

> A user who genuinely finishes setup for meeting-only or continuous listening must have the app running again after a Mac restart, so automatic detection and capture continue without a manual relaunch.

The current helper and tests misdescribe that lifecycle requirement as an active user choice. No such choice exists in the active UI.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Enable Launch at Login after genuine completion.** Both retained listening modes need the app running after restart. Disclose this on the final listening screen, let Settings turn it off later, and do not enable it after global Skip.
2. **Add a Launch at Login choice to active onboarding.** Create a new concrete screen/toggle, default it on, then apply the explicit answer at completion. This adds another onboarding step.
3. **Move ownership entirely to Settings.** Normal completion leaves the login item untouched; users must discover and enable it themselves, so automatic listening can silently stop after a restart.
4. **Keep the current invisible snapshot replay.** Continue writing the one-time snapshot at completion even though the user did not select it and the snapshot can be stale.

### Recommendation

`enable Launch at Login after genuine completion, disclose it, preserve the Settings off-switch, and leave it off after global Skip`

Launch at Login is not unrelated to the retained listening lifecycle. If the app is not running after reboot, meeting-only detection and continuous listening cannot happen. The simplest reliable behavior is explicit and truthful: genuine completion directly calls `setEnabled(true)`, the final listening screen says the app will open at login and can be disabled in Settings, and global Skip does not register it.

Delete the unused `launchAtLogin` snapshot and `applyLaunchAtLoginSelection()` abstraction because they pretend to preserve a missing choice. Replace their focused tests with the real contract: genuine completion requests enablement; global Skip does not; Settings remains the observed user-controlled off-switch. Keep completion-source analytics only for a successful real registration.

### Question

Should genuine onboarding completion explicitly enable Launch at Login so the retained meeting-only/continuous listening lifecycle survives a Mac restart, with truthful disclosure on the final screen, no enablement after global Skip, and the existing Settings toggle available to turn it off?

### Decision

`resolved - enable Launch at Login after genuine completion; disclose it; leave it off after global Skip; keep the Settings off-switch`

Retain automatic startup for users who genuinely choose meeting-only or continuous listening so those modes keep working after a Mac restart. Remove the stale `launchAtLogin` snapshot and the helper that pretends to replay an onboarding choice. Genuine completion directly requests enablement and reports success; global Skip must not register the login item. The final listening screen must disclose that the app will open at login and that the existing Settings control can turn it off.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-146 - One-time Launch at Login migration for already-onboarded profiles

### Exact current behavior from the code

Every app launch calls `migrateLaunchAtLoginDefault()` before applying the separate relaunch policy. The method:

1. checks the local `didMigrateLaunchAtLoginV1` marker and returns if it already ran;
2. immediately marks the migration complete;
3. returns unless the local profile already has `hasCompletedOnboarding = true`;
4. reads `LaunchAtLoginManager.isEnabled`; and
5. if that value is false, registers the app as a login item and reports **Launch At Login Changed** with source `migration`.

This path cannot distinguish **never enabled** from **the user deliberately disabled it in macOS Settings**. It also reads the manager's initially-false published value while the real `SMAppService` status is loaded asynchronously.

### Requirement materialized by this migration

> When Launch at Login is introduced to an already-shipped installed population, automatically backfill it once for users who completed onboarding before normal completion owned that behavior.

Our new product has no shipped legacy population requiring this backfill. IR-145 now makes genuine completion the authority for new users, while the retained Settings toggle owns later user changes.

### Decision

`resolved - delete the one-time legacy Launch at Login migration`

Delete the startup call, `migrateLaunchAtLoginDefault()`, the `didMigrateLaunchAtLoginV1` marker, and migration-source analytics path. Do not alter the retained `LaunchAtLoginManager`, genuine-completion enablement under IR-145, global-Skip exclusion, or the Settings toggle.

## IR-147 - AppKit reopen-at-login policy beside the retained login item

### Exact current behavior from the code

This is separate from the `SMAppService` Launch at Login setting reviewed under IR-145.

macOS can reopen an application at the next login when that application was still running at logout. AppKit exposes a process-local counter through `NSApp.disableRelaunchOnLogin()` and `enableRelaunchOnLogin()`:

- counter zero: macOS may reopen the app that was running at logout;
- counter above zero: suppress that automatic reopening.

The current app calls `updateOnboardingLifecyclePolicy()` at launch and after every `UserDefaults.didChangeNotification`:

- non-production bundles call `disableRelaunchOnLogin()`;
- production before onboarding completion calls `disableRelaunchOnLogin()`; and
- production after onboarding completion calls `enableRelaunchOnLogin()`.

Therefore a genuinely onboarded production user currently has two independent routes that can reopen the app:

```text
SMAppService login item
  -> controlled by genuine onboarding + the visible Settings toggle

AppKit reopen-if-running-at-logout
  -> enabled automatically after onboarding
  -> not controlled by the visible Settings toggle
```

If the user turns **Launch at Login** off in Settings but leaves the app running when logging out, AppKit may still reopen it next time. The visible off-switch is therefore not the only authority.

The macOS SDK contract recommends calling `disableRelaunchOnLogin()` once and never pairing it with `enableRelaunchOnLogin()` when the application already launches through another mechanism. The retained `SMAppService` login item is our explicit mechanism.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Use only the retained `SMAppService` login item.** Call `disableRelaunchOnLogin()` once during app startup for every bundle, delete the onboarding/UserDefaults-driven enable/disable policy, and make genuine completion plus Settings the single automatic-start authority.
2. **Keep both relaunch mechanisms.** After onboarding, macOS may restore an app that was running at logout even when the visible Launch at Login setting is off.
3. **Delete the `SMAppService` login item and use only AppKit restoration.** This would remove the explicit, observable Settings preference retained under IR-145 and would only reopen the app if it happened to be running at logout.

### Recommendation

`suppress AppKit's independent relaunch path once at startup and rely only on the retained SMAppService login item`

This gives automatic startup one owner. Genuine completion enables it, global Skip leaves it off, and Settings can reliably disable it. Meeting-only and continuous listening still survive restart when Launch at Login is enabled; the extra AppKit route adds no retained capability.

Delete `updateOnboardingLifecyclePolicy()`, its `UserDefaults.didChangeNotification` observer, and `relaunchOnLoginSuppressedForOnboarding`. Replace them with one startup call to `NSApp.disableRelaunchOnLogin()`.

### Question

Should we suppress AppKit's separate reopen-if-running-at-logout behavior once at startup and rely only on the retained `SMAppService` Launch at Login setting?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the current AppKit reopen-at-login policy unchanged`

Retain `updateOnboardingLifecyclePolicy()`, its `UserDefaults.didChangeNotification` observer, and `relaunchOnLoginSuppressedForOnboarding`. Production builds continue to suppress AppKit reopening before onboarding and allow it after onboarding; non-production bundles continue to suppress it. Keep this behavior alongside the retained `SMAppService` login item and its Settings control.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-148 - Proactive screen monitoring enabled by genuine onboarding completion

### Exact current behavior from the code

Normal `SBOnboardingModel.complete()` treats proactive screen monitoring separately from the final meeting-only/continuous audio choice. In a normal production build it always:

1. writes `AssistantSettings.screenAnalysisEnabled = true`; and
2. calls `ProactiveAssistantsPlugin.startMonitoring()` if monitoring is not already running.

This happens for both final audio choices and does not inspect the earlier onboarding `scrState`:

- if Screen Recording permission was granted, monitoring can start immediately;
- if that screen was skipped, the plugin retries permission checks without opening the macOS permission prompt, then gives up while the stored screen-analysis intent remains enabled; and
- Home can try again later through persisted-intent restoration after permission or provider readiness changes.

Global Skip remains a separate no-capture path under IR-127 and must not inherit this behavior.

### Requirement materialized by this completion side effect

> A user who genuinely completes onboarding should enter the retained proactive-assistant/Rewind experience with screen monitoring enabled whenever macOS permission is available, independent of whether they selected meeting-only or continuous audio listening.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Keep the current completion default.** Genuine completion records screen-analysis intent as enabled and starts monitoring when permission is available. The earlier Screen Recording step remains the consent boundary; skipping it prevents capture because macOS permission is absent. Global Skip leaves intent off.
2. **Treat the Screen Recording step's answer as the durable intent.** Completion enables monitoring only when `scrState == .on`; choosing **Skip** on that individual screen stores screen analysis off until the user enables it later in Settings.
3. **Delete automatic screen monitoring.** Retain Screen Recording only for explicit PTT screenshot tools and require a later manual action to enable proactive/Rewind monitoring. This weakens the proactive overlay and Rewind/Focus behavior already retained.

### Recommendation

`keep the current genuine-completion behavior, while keeping global Skip as the distinct no-screen-monitoring outcome`

The active onboarding already explains and requests Screen Recording before completion, and macOS permission remains the hard capture boundary. The retained proactive overlay plus Rewind/Focus need ongoing screen observation. Keep normal completion's enabled intent and permission-gated start rather than adding another durable interpretation of the individual **Skip for now** button.

### Question

Should genuine onboarding completion continue enabling proactive screen monitoring whenever Screen Recording permission is available, for both meeting-only and continuous audio modes, while global Skip remains the distinct no-monitoring outcome?

### Decision

`resolved - keep genuine-completion proactive screen monitoring unchanged`

For both retained meeting-only and continuous audio modes, genuine completion continues to record screen-analysis intent as enabled and start monitoring when Screen Recording permission is available. If permission is absent, the plugin may retry without opening the macOS permission prompt and Home may reconcile the stored intent later. Global Skip remains the distinct no-monitoring outcome under IR-127.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-149 - Resume incomplete onboarding from a local stage marker

### Exact current behavior from the code

Every normal forward or Back transition stores the destination step's integer value in local `UserDefaults` under `sbOnboardingResumeStep`. Genuine completion and global Skip delete that marker.

When incomplete onboarding appears after an app relaunch, `SBOnboardingModel.begin()`:

1. restores editable name/language/role drafts from their existing stores;
2. reads the saved local stage;
3. re-enters that stage instead of replaying every earlier screen; and
4. if the saved stage is a permission the user granted while the app was away, skips forward to the first stage that still needs an answer.

It does not restore the entire decorative conversational transcript. It restores the actionable stage and saved answers. No backend or cloud synchronization is involved.

### Requirement materialized by this behavior

> Quitting or restarting the app during setup must not force the user to repeat completed onboarding screens, especially when macOS permission work interrupted the flow.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Keep local stage resume.** Preserve the small `UserDefaults` marker, draft rehydration, permission recheck, and completion/Skip cleanup.
2. **Always restart from the opening screen.** Delete the marker and restoration logic; previously saved answers and granted permissions may prefill or auto-skip, but the user still traverses setup again.
3. **Persist the full onboarding chat transcript.** Restore every decorative bubble as well as the current widget. This adds storage/state complexity without restoring additional product work.

### Recommendation

`keep the current lightweight local stage resume`

Permission setup commonly sends the user to System Settings and can involve restarting the app. The current mechanism is local, small, and resumes only actionable state rather than persisting unnecessary conversational presentation.

### Question

Should incomplete onboarding continue resuming from its locally saved stage after relaunch, rechecking permissions and keeping completion/Skip responsible for clearing the marker?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the lightweight local onboarding stage resume unchanged`

Retain `sbOnboardingResumeStep`, draft rehydration, already-granted-permission skipping, and marker cleanup on genuine completion or global Skip. Do not persist the decorative conversational transcript or add cloud synchronization.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-150 - One-step Back navigation throughout active onboarding

### Exact current behavior from the code

Every stage after the opening promise shows a top-right **Back** button beside global **Skip**. Pressing it:

1. tears down live work owned by the current stage, including file scans, shortcut monitors, or the screen-aware voice demo;
2. cancels the current permission poll;
3. reloads editable drafts from their saved stores;
4. moves to the immediately preceding enum stage;
5. saves that prior stage as the local resume point; and
6. streams the prior stage's assistant prompt again while keeping the existing conversational transcript visible.

Returning does not roll back work that cannot truthfully be undone by navigation. A macOS permission remains granted, and a previously saved name/language/shortcut remains stored until the user submits a replacement. The re-rendered widget shows the current state and lets editable answers be revised.

Deleted screens under IR-131/135/137/141/142 must also disappear from this stage order, so Back moves through only retained onboarding stages.

### Requirement materialized by this behavior

> A user must be able to revisit and revise the immediately preceding onboarding answer without restarting setup, while leaving operating-system grants and already-completed external effects truthful.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Keep one-step Back.** Preserve the button, local resume update, editable-answer restoration, and current-stage teardown. Do not pretend navigation can revoke macOS permissions.
2. **Remove Back.** Users can only move forward or abandon the entire flow with global Skip; correcting an earlier name, language, or shortcut requires restarting onboarding or finding a later Settings control.
3. **Build transactional rollback.** Attempt to reverse every prior answer and permission when navigating backward. macOS grants cannot be programmatically revoked, so this would create a misleading and complex partial rollback.

### Recommendation

`keep the current one-step Back behavior`

The retained onboarding still has enough screens that accidental choices need a cheap correction path. Current teardown prevents live monitors from leaking across stages, while truthful non-rollback of macOS grants avoids pretending the app controls System Settings.

### Question

Should onboarding keep the current Back button on every stage after the opening screen, allowing prior editable answers to be revised while macOS permissions remain unchanged?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the current one-step Back behavior unchanged`

Retain the Back button, current-step teardown, cancellation of permission polling, draft rehydration, and update of the local resume marker. Going Back may revise editable answers but does not pretend to revoke macOS permissions or reverse already-completed external effects.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-151 - Simulated typing for fixed local onboarding prompts

### Exact current behavior from the code

Each onboarding prompt is fixed copy returned locally by `message(for:)`; it is not generated by a model and it does not arrive from a server. Even so, `streamMessage(for:)` presents every prompt as if Omi were composing it live:

1. hide the screen's controls;
2. wait 700 milliseconds while showing **omi is typing…**;
3. reveal one or two words at a time with a random 55–150 millisecond wait between updates;
4. append the completed prompt to the visible conversation; and only then
5. show the controls and begin that stage's real work, such as checking a permission.

The same delay runs after normal forward navigation, Back navigation, and restoration of an incomplete stage. The implementation requires cancellable task state plus separate `typing`, `streamingText`, and `showWidget` presentation states. This mechanism is separate from an actual PTT/model response in the retained live demo.

### Requirement materialized by this behavior

> Fixed onboarding copy must imitate a live conversational reply before the user can interact with each stage.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Remove the simulated typing.** Render the retained prompt and its controls immediately, and start the stage's real setup work immediately. Keep actual model-response streaming where real output is arriving over time.
2. **Keep it unchanged.** Preserve the typing indicator, random word reveal, delayed controls, cancellable task state, and repeated animation when revisiting a stage.
3. **Shorten the animation.** Reduce the waits but retain the extra presentation states and cancellation lifecycle.

### Recommendation

`remove the simulated typing for fixed local onboarding copy`

It makes every retained setup step slower while communicating something untrue: no assistant is thinking or generating that copy. Showing the prompt and controls immediately removes waiting and state without removing any setup requirement, explanation, or real model behavior.

### Question

Should we remove the fake word-by-word typing animation from fixed onboarding copy and show each retained prompt and its controls immediately, while keeping real streaming for the actual live PTT/model demo?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the current simulated typing behavior unchanged`

Retain the 700-millisecond typing state, word-by-word prompt reveal, delayed widget presentation, cancellable task state, and the same behavior when a stage is revisited. This decision applies only to the fixed onboarding presentation and does not change actual live model streaming.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-152 - No progress indicator in conversational onboarding

### Exact current behavior from the code

The onboarding panel deliberately contains no progress dots, progress bar, step number, or “step X of Y” copy. Beneath the scrolling conversation it renders only a 14-point clear spacer. A source comment states that the user should not count steps or feel a finish line.

The user can see the accumulated conversation, the current prompt, **Back**, and global **Skip**, but cannot see how many setup stages remain. The actual path is conditional: already-granted permissions can be skipped automatically, and the retained product will also remove stages rejected elsewhere in this review.

1. **Keep no progress indicator.** Preserve the current conversational presentation and conditional traversal without introducing progress calculation or another UI element.
2. **Add exact progress.** Show a count or bar based on the retained stages. It would need to account for permissions that may be skipped and for every stage removed by this review.
3. **Add coarse progress.** Show broad phases such as Profile, Permissions, and Try Omi without promising an exact number of screens.

### Recommendation

`keep the current no-progress presentation unchanged`

The path is conditional, so an exact count would either jump when granted permissions are skipped or require additional progress rules. We are already shortening the journey by deleting rejected stages, and the existing Back and Skip controls prevent the user from being trapped. Adding a new indicator does not help simplify or ship this fork.

### Question

Should the onboarding continue showing no progress dots, step count, or finish line, exactly as it does now?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the current no-progress presentation unchanged`

Retain the conversational panel without dots, a progress bar, step numbering, or a finish line. Do not add progress calculation for conditional or already-granted-permission skips.

## IR-153 - In-memory conversation history during onboarding

### Exact current behavior from the code

During one onboarding session, the panel behaves like a chat transcript:

1. each completed fixed Omi prompt is appended to an in-memory `thread` array;
2. a submitted answer is appended as a right-aligned user bubble when the stage supplies non-empty answer text;
3. the panel automatically scrolls to the newest prompt, answer, streamed text, or widget; and
4. all earlier bubbles remain visible above the current stage.

This transcript is presentation state, not durable user data. It is not written to a database or synchronized to a backend. After an app restart, IR-149 restores only the actionable stage and saved drafts, not the prior bubbles.

Back navigation also leaves the existing bubbles intact. It appends the earlier prompt again and may later append a revised answer, so the visible history can contain both the old and revised answer even though the re-rendered widget and saved store represent the current value.

### Requirement materialized by this behavior

> Onboarding must look and read like an accumulating conversation during the current app session, rather than replacing the panel with one setup card at a time.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Keep the current in-memory transcript.** Preserve accumulated prompt and answer bubbles, automatic scrolling, and the current Back behavior. Persist only the actionable state already retained under IR-149.
2. **Show only the current stage.** Remove the `thread` collection and earlier bubbles, leaving the current fixed prompt and widget. This is a simpler wizard-like presentation but abandons the existing conversational experience.
3. **Make Back rewrite history.** Keep the transcript but remove or replace superseded prompts and answers when revisiting stages. This adds transcript-to-stage bookkeeping solely to make decorative history appear canonical.

### Recommendation

`keep the current in-memory transcript unchanged`

The decisions to retain simulated typing and the no-progress conversational presentation make the current-session history part of one coherent experience. It is small, local, and automatically discarded; rewriting it around Back would add more state than it removes. The active widget and saved local value remain authoritative when an answer is revised.

### Question

Should onboarding keep its current in-memory scrolling conversation exactly as it is, including leaving old prompt and answer bubbles visible when the user goes Back and changes an answer?

### Decision

`resolved - keep the current in-memory onboarding conversation unchanged`

Retain the scrolling, session-only prompt and answer history, automatic scrolling, and current Back behavior. Do not persist this decorative transcript or add logic that rewrites old bubbles after an answer changes; the active widget and locally saved value remain authoritative.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-154 - Superseded 18-page onboarding implementation

### Exact current behavior from the code

The shipping app has two substantial onboarding implementations:

1. `DesktopHomeView` routes every signed-in, not-yet-onboarded production user to `SBOnboardingView`, the conversational flow reviewed under IR-125–153.
2. The older `OnboardingView` still defines an independent 18-page wizard with its own step list, phase progress, navigation rules, migration flags, coordinator, permission pages, demos, connector pages, goal/task pages, and completion lifecycle.

No production UI route instantiates the old `OnboardingView`. Its remaining direct construction is in `ViewExporter`, which renders screenshots of the old 18 pages for developer visual exports. A separate set of tests continues to protect this old flow and its migrations.

Some non-UI helpers currently live beside or inside the legacy system and still have live callers. For example, the conversational flow uses `OnboardingAnswerWriteGate`; sign-out/reset uses `OnboardingFlow.clearPersistedState()`; Settings reads the legacy coordinator's common-language list; and some connector/import helpers are used outside onboarding. Those live primitives must be kept or moved until their own requirements are reviewed. “Delete the old renderer” does not mean blindly deleting every file whose name starts with `Onboarding`.

### Requirement materialized by this behavior

> The product must maintain a complete second onboarding experience, which customers cannot enter, so developers can export screenshots of the superseded pages and keep its old-flow tests passing.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Delete the superseded paged experience.** Remove `OnboardingView`, its page-only views/coordinator branches, its old screenshot-export registry, its migration-only state, and tests that protect only that dead experience. First extract or retain any small helper with a proven current caller.
2. **Keep both onboarding systems.** Continue compiling, testing, and adapting the old 18-page implementation alongside the one customers actually use.
3. **Restore a runtime switch between them.** Add product/configuration complexity so some users or developers can enter either onboarding experience.

### Recommendation

`delete the superseded paged onboarding experience, preserving only proven live dependencies`

The screenshot exporter is not a customer requirement and currently preserves a large second product surface. Every local/cloud architecture change would otherwise have to be understood in both implementations even though only one can ship. Removing the dead renderer is a high-leverage simplification; tracing live helper callers first keeps the deletion precise rather than reckless.

### Question

Should we delete the superseded 18-page `OnboardingView` experience and its old screenshot/test surface, while extracting or retaining only helpers that the current conversational onboarding or post-onboarding app still uses?

### Decision

`resolved - delete the superseded paged onboarding experience`

Delete `OnboardingView`, page-only views and coordinator branches, old step navigation and migrations, the 18-page screenshot-export registry, and tests that protect only the unreachable experience. Before removal, trace every referenced helper: preserve or extract only code with a current caller in conversational onboarding, Settings, sign-out/reset, post-onboarding UI, or another retained product surface.

## IR-155 - Local onboarding-state cleanup on sign-out and reset

### Exact current behavior from the code

The legacy `OnboardingFlow` type owns a shared list of local `UserDefaults` keys. Two live paths call its `clearPersistedState()` function:

1. **Sign out:** after revoking the current account session, the app clears local onboarding keys and legacy onboarding-chat persistence so another account on the same Mac does not inherit the prior account's setup stage.
2. **Reset Onboarding:** the app marks onboarding incomplete, clears the same local keys and setup-owned conversation state, then restarts the current app build so the conversational setup opens again.

The reset deliberately does not revoke macOS permissions or erase normal chat/product data. Those are separate authorities and are not undone merely because the user wants to replay setup.

The current cleanup list mixes live conversational keys with obsolete paged-flow keys. For example, `sbOnboardingResumeStep` and `onboardingJustCompleted` still belong to the current path, while old page indexes, furthest-step state, deleted role/goal state, and several historical trigger flags may disappear with IR-154 or other decisions. The cleanup behavior is live even though its current owner contains dead legacy machinery.

### Requirement materialized by this behavior

> Account-scoped local onboarding state must not leak to the next signed-in account, and an explicit onboarding reset must restart the current setup without destroying normal user data or pretending to revoke macOS permissions.

### Choices for this concrete behavior

1. **Keep a narrowed shared cleanup boundary.** Move or rename the cleanup owner, retain only current conversational-onboarding keys and setup-owned local state, and keep both sign-out and Reset Onboarding calling it.
2. **Delete onboarding cleanup with the old flow.** Sign-out or reset may leave the resume stage, completion opener, or other setup state behind for the next account or replay.
3. **Make reset a broad data wipe.** Clear normal chat, product data, settings, or permissions as well as onboarding state; this would be destructive and would not actually revoke macOS TCC permissions.

### Recommendation

`keep the shared cleanup behavior, but narrow it to the retained conversational onboarding state`

This is local ownership hygiene, not cloud synchronization or a second onboarding system. Deleting the legacy owner should remove obsolete keys and persistence, while a small current-flow cleanup primitive prevents cross-account state leakage and makes Reset Onboarding truthful.

### Question

Should sign-out and Reset Onboarding continue clearing only the retained account-scoped onboarding state through one small shared local helper, while leaving normal app data and macOS permissions untouched?

### Decision

`resolved - keep a narrowed shared local onboarding-state cleanup boundary`

Sign-out and Reset Onboarding continue calling one small helper that clears retained account-scoped setup state and setup-owned local conversation state. Remove obsolete paged-flow keys and legacy persistence as their owners are deleted. Do not erase normal app data or claim to revoke macOS permissions.

No code deletion is authorized yet.

## IR-156 - User-facing Reset Onboarding capability

### Decision

`resolved - keep the confirmed Reset Onboarding capability in Advanced Settings`

Completed users retain the explicit Settings recovery path. After confirmation it clears only retained setup state, restarts the current app build, and replays conversational onboarding without erasing normal data or claiming to revoke macOS permissions.
